rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 4-7 report a greenhouse experiment (Tongzhou station, 2016) with cucumber and tomato under subsurface drip with micro-nano bubble water, nine treatments, four replications, own yield, IWUE, quality and soil-oxygen measurements.
rows.notes: The study does not show water or fertilizer saving or soil-moisture conservation: Section 2.2 and Table 3 state that irrigation quota and fertilizer were identical in all treatments, soil water content was assumed (not measured) to be approximately equal (Section 3.2), and the reported gain is in yield and in IWUE at constant water. The abstract phrases this as increased IWUE 'without increasing' water and fertilizer, which is not evidence of saving water or conserving soil moisture as the passage claims. Technology (MNB oxygation through SDI) is a form of aerated drip, so no technology mismatch. Also unclear whether this paper is the review's Liu et al. 2019a or 2019b.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, greenhouse experiment with own measurements of yield, IWUE, quality and soil oxygen. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report IWUE of tomato and cucumber significantly higher under MNB oxygation than the non-oxygated SDI control at equal irrigation quota (e.g. tomato IWUE 24.8 vs 20.3 kg/m3 in autumn under F1/5; abstract: IWUE up 16.9% tomato, 22.1% cucumber). Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 measure soil oxygen content in the root zone for three mixing ratios and Section 4.1 reports higher, stable soil oxygen under oxygation; Table 4 reports root dry weight, the intermediate through which aeration raises yield and hence IWUE. Q9: Table 5 reports IWUE means with <U+00B1> dispersion values for every treatment and season.
rows.notes: Evidence for 'water conservation' is only the IWUE (yield per unit irrigation water) increase; applied water was identical across treatments and soil water was not measured, so the study shows more yield per unit water rather than reduced water use. Q3: single method (plot yield divided by applied water). Q5: one site, one loam soil, two crops. Q6: greenhouse plots only. Q7: authors recommend an optimal mixing ratio and 5-d frequency and speculate that 7-d frequency lets bubbles escape, but do not state a condition required for the effect; effects were positive at all frequencies. Q8: no limitation stated for the IWUE/yield result (only quality mechanism flagged for further study).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own greenhouse experiment with nine MNB-oxygation treatments and a non-oxygated SDI control. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report tomato yield up to 16.9% and cucumber yield up to 22.1% higher than control under oxygation at the 5-d frequency, with significant letter groupings; Section 4.1 summarises yield gains of 7.8-26.9% (tomato) and 2.3-16.3% (cucumber). Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 measure root-zone soil oxygen content under the three mixing ratios, showing higher and stable soil oxygen under oxygation; Table 4 reports root and shoot dry matter, the intermediate through which the yield gain occurs. Q9: Table 5 gives yield means with <U+00B1> dispersion for every treatment in spring and autumn.
rows.notes: Q3: yield measured by one method only. Q5: one greenhouse, one loam soil, two crops (cucumber, tomato) <U+2013> fewer than three distinct contexts. Q6: 6 m x 3 m plots in a single greenhouse. Q7: recommended mixing ratio and frequency are given, and 7-d frequency is argued to be overly long, but these are reported as variations/recommendations rather than conditions required for the effect. Q8: no stated limitation on the yield result; the only self-identified gaps concern the fruit-quality mechanism and the mixing-ratio gradient.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own greenhouse experiment. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report both yield and IWUE of tomato and cucumber significantly higher under MNB oxygation than under non-oxygated SDI (abstract: yield and IWUE up 16.9% tomato, 22.1% cucumber in optimal treatment); Section 3.2 explains IWUE followed yield because irrigation quota was equal. Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 measure root-zone soil oxygen under different mixing ratios and Section 4.1 links the higher, stable soil oxygen to the yield/IWUE gain; Table 4 reports root dry matter. Q9: Table 5 reports <U+00B1> dispersion values for yield and WUE in each treatment and season.
rows.notes: Claim (aeration boosts yield while increasing WUE) matches the study's main result. Q3: one method only. Q5: single site/soil, two crops. Q6: plot scale in one greenhouse. Q7: optimal mode recommended but no requirement stated. Q8: no limitations stated for the yield/IWUE result beyond 'further investigation' of quality mechanisms.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a single-season-pair (spring and autumn 2016) greenhouse trial at one site on loam soil; MNB water delivered through subsurface drip is treated as a form of aerated drip irrigation for all rows.
